29.title: Lost for three days (Luke 2:41–52)
29.hook: twelve-year-old Jesus stays in the Temple and asks why they didn't know he'd be in his Father's house
29.howItsDone: Catholics meditate on this story as the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the Finding in the Temple, and as one of the Seven Sorrows of Mary; it is read on the feast of the Holy Family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epiphany, strangers from the east, and then a family running for Egypt. The holy family were refugees. Week five begins: the beginning.
screen: `THE HOLY FAMILY WERE REFUGEES.` → `WEEK FIVE: THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: A parent turns around in a crowded market, and the child isn't there. Now stretch that moment to three days. Every year, Luke says, Mary and Joseph walked to Jerusalem for the Passover in a big crowd of relatives and neighbors. The year Jesus is twelve, they start home assuming he's somewhere in the caravan with the cousins. A whole day's walk later, they realize he isn't. They turn back and search Jerusalem. One day. Two. Three.
screen: `YOU TURN AROUND. HE'S GONE.` → `A DAY'S WALK BEFORE THEY NOTICE.` → `ONE DAY. TWO. THREE.`

segments.voice: They find him, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, the scholars of the law. A twelve-year-old from a village sits among them, and Luke says everyone was astonished at how he understood and how he answered. Mary says what a frightened parent says: "Son, why hast thou done so to us? behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Sorrowing: three days of it. His answer is the first thing Jesus says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that you sought me? did you not know, that I must be about my father's business?" In Luke's Greek the phrase is short and open: in the things of my Father. Older English Bibles say business; some newer ones say house. Both are possible. Either way: I'm where I belong. Luke admits they didn't understand him, not even Mary. He goes home with them and obeys them, and Mary keeps all these things in her heart, the same words Luke used after the shepherds. Catholics hold this story in two places at once. It's the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the finding in the Temple: a joy. And it's one of the seven sorrows of Mary. Notice where they found him. Not playing, not lost and crying. Asking questions. It's his first scene past babyhood, and in it, questions aren't the opposite of faith.
screen: `SITTING AMONG THE TEACHERS.` · `THY FATHER AND I HAVE SOUGHT THEE.` · `IN THE THINGS OF MY FATHER.` · `A JOY AND A SORROW.` · then, large: `THEY FOUND HIM ASKING QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you once lost: for a few minutes in a crowd, for years to a falling-out, or for good. Remember what the searching felt like, without hurrying past it. If they were found, remember that moment too; if not, hold them gently, and if you pray, bring them to God.
Doctors. In Luke's story, the teachers of the law in the Temple, where the boy sat listening and asking.
Your line: they found him asking questions. Not lost, not crying: asking. See you tomorrow.

30.title: The hidden years
30.hook: thirty years in Nazareth, a trade, a village, nothing written down
30.carry: most of his life was ordinary
30.howItsDone: Catholics honor the hidden life of Jesus on the feast of the Holy Family, after Christmas, and on the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, May 1; many religious communities take Nazareth as a model of prayerful ordinary work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the doctors, the Temple's teachers, and a boy of twelve found among them asking questions. Today, what comes after: almost nothing at all.

A biography keeps the graduation, the wedding, the big move. It skips the ten thousand Tuesdays: the dishes, the commute, the afternoon someone fixed a chair. The Gospels go further. There's the birth. There's one story at twelve. Then the next time Jesus appears, Luke says he's about thirty. About eighteen years without a single scene. Catholics have a name for that silence: the hidden life.
screen: `NOT THE TEN THOUSAND TUESDAYS.` → `TWELVE, THEN THIRTY.` → `EIGHTEEN YEARS, NO SCENES.`

segments.voice: What's known is very little. Luke gives two sentences. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them." And: "Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men." Grace, your very first word, again. He grew, the way children grow. Mark adds one clue, years later, when the people of Nazareth are offended by him: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" The Greek word is tekton: a builder, a craftsman in wood or stone. So it's possible to guess at a life. A small village. A family trade, likely learned from Joseph. Rough hands, customers who paid late, neighbors' weddings and funerals. Probably Joseph's death somewhere in there, since he disappears from the story. But those are guesses; the Gospels are silent. Later writers couldn't stand the silence, and stories appeared of a boy Jesus making clay birds fly and doing flashy miracles. The Church never accepted them as scripture. The real tradition kept the silence, and found something in it. If Jesus is who Catholics believe he is, then God spent about thirty years, of a life tradition counts at about thirty-three, doing ordinary work in a village no one had heard of. Hidden, and not wasted. A French hermit named Charles de Foucauld, now a saint, spent years trying to live just like that, and called it living Nazareth. Sawing a board carefully counts.
screen: `TWO SENTENCES FROM LUKE.` · `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` · `THE GOSPELS ARE SILENT.` · `LIVING NAZARETH.` · then, large: `MOST OF HIS LIFE WAS ORDINARY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the most ordinary task ahead of you today: washing a pan, folding a shirt, driving the same road. Picture doing it slowly and well, the way a craftsman planes a board, with no one watching. If you pray, offer it to God before you begin.
Tekton. Mark's Greek word for Jesus's trade: a builder in wood or stone, perhaps taught by Joseph in Nazareth.
Your line: most of his life was ordinary. Eighteen quiet years, and they counted. Day thirty, done.

31.title: The voice in the desert (Matthew 3:1–12)
31.hook: John the Baptist in camel hair, eating locusts, calling people to turn around
31.howItsDone: Catholics hear John the Baptist's call in the Advent Sunday readings and answer it in the sacrament of penance (confession), where a person names their sins, receives absolution and is given a penance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tekton, the builder's trade, and eighteen quiet years in Nazareth. Today the quiet ends with a shout from the desert.

Out past the towns, in the dry country near the Jordan River, a man is shouting. He wears a rough garment of camel's hair with a leather belt. He eats locusts and wild honey. No house, no title, no invitation. And people come, Matthew says, from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan. They stand in the river, confess their sins, and he baptizes them. This is John, the one Christians call the Baptist, a relative of Jesus. His message fits in one breath.
screen: `A MAN SHOUTING IN THE DESERT.` → `CAMEL HAIR, LOCUSTS, WILD HONEY.` → `AND THE CROWDS COME.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims Bible, the old Catholic English translation: "Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." The King James says repent. Both reach for one Greek word, metanoia. Meta, after or beyond. Noia, from the word for mind. A change of mind, a turning around. Not feeling bad, first of all: a new direction. The Douay-Rheims followed the Latin Bible's do penance, and that wording is one reason Catholics speak of the sacrament of penance: confession carries an echo of this call. Matthew hears John in the prophet Isaiah, centuries earlier: "A voice of one crying in the desert, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." Isaiah pictures a road made ready for a king: low places filled, hills brought down, the crooked made straight. John's message: a king is coming, and the road is you. He isn't gentle about it. When religious leaders come to watch, he tells them to bring forth fruit worthy of penance, to show the turning in how they live. The axe, he says, is already at the root of the trees. But he points away from himself. Someone mightier is coming after him, and John isn't worthy even to carry his sandals. The Church keeps John close. His voice fills the Sundays of Advent, and both his birth, on June twenty-fourth, and his death have their own feasts.
screen: `DO PENANCE: THE KINGDOM IS AT HAND.` · `METANOIA — A CHANGE OF MIND.` · `A KING IS COMING. FIX THE ROAD.` · `HE POINTS AWAY FROM HIMSELF.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let one thing come to mind that you'd like to turn from: a habit that keeps the road crooked, a sharp way of talking, a grudge you keep feeding. Name it plainly, inside, without trying to fix it yet. If you pray, hold it up to God and ask for help turning; if you don't, just sit with the naming.
Metanoia. Greek for a change of mind, a turning around: John's call at the Jordan.
Your line: make straight the way. The road John meant runs through a life. Thirty-one days in.

32.title: The baptism (Matthew 3:13–17)
32.hook: Jesus steps into the line of sinners, the sky opens, a voice says beloved
32.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Baptism of the Lord as the feast that ends the Christmas season, pray it as the first Luminous Mystery of the rosary, and bless themselves with holy water on entering a church as a reminder of their own baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday: metanoia, a turning around, and John's voice in the desert clearing the road for someone greater.

A long line at the river. Everyone in it is there for the same reason: they've done things they regret, and they want to turn around. A tax man. A soldier. A woman who hasn't spoken to her sister in years. Nobody in that line is showing off. Then a carpenter from Nazareth steps in and waits his turn like everybody else. When he reaches the front, John looks at him and stops. He knows who this is, and he tries to refuse.
screen: `A LINE OF PEOPLE WITH REGRETS.` → `A CARPENTER STEPS INTO LINE.` → `JOHN TRIES TO REFUSE.`

segments.voice: John's words, in the Douay-Rheims: "I ought to be baptized by thee, and comest thou to me?" It's backward, he means: you should be baptizing me. Jesus answers that it is fitting, for now, to fulfill all justice, and John lets him come down into the river. Why get in line at all? Christians have asked that for two thousand years. The Church's answer: not for his own sins. He was standing where sinners stand, on purpose, in the water with them. Then the story opens up. As he comes out, Matthew says, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God coming down like a dove and resting on him. And a voice from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Look at the timing. Before a single miracle, sermon, follower or healing, he's already beloved. The Church reads the scene as a window onto the Trinity: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice. The feast of the Baptism of the Lord closes the Christmas season, and it's the first of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary. Catholics hear their own baptism in it too: the Catechism teaches that baptism makes a person an adopted child of God. That's why there's holy water at the church door. People dip their fingers and make the sign of the cross on the way in, remembering the water they came through.
screen: `JOHN: YOU SHOULD BAPTIZE ME.` · `HE STANDS WHERE SINNERS STAND.` · `BELOVED, BEFORE HE DOES ANYTHING.` · `HOLY WATER AT THE CHURCH DOOR.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: If you can, touch a little water from a glass or a tap, and feel how cool or warm it is; a Catholic might make the sign of the cross, as at the church door; if not, just let the water be water. Then sit, and let one sentence rest on you: loved, before doing anything.
The baptism. Jesus steps into the river with sinners, and a voice from heaven calls him beloved.
Your line: you are the beloved. Loved first, before any of the day's work. Until tomorrow.

33.title: Forty days hungry (Matthew 4:1–11)
33.hook: bread, a leap, the kingdoms of the world, three temptations and three refusals
33.howItsDone: Catholics keep Lent as forty days of prayer, fasting and almsgiving; the Gospel on the First Sunday of Lent is the temptation in the desert, and many give up a comfort for the season.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the baptism, and a voice calling Jesus beloved before he'd done anything. From the river, Matthew says, he goes straight into the desert.

Afterwards he was hungry. That's all Matthew says about forty days and forty nights without food, after the spirit led Jesus into the desert. Not a missed lunch: the kind of hunger where the head goes light and every thought bends toward bread. And that's exactly when the tempter comes. Not on day one, when he's strong. At the end, when he's weakest. Three offers, one after another.
screen: `FORTY DAYS, FORTY NIGHTS.` → `AFTERWARD HE WAS HUNGRY.` → `THEN THE TEMPTER COMES.`

segments.voice: First, bread. If you are the Son of God, the tempter says, tell these stones to become loaves. It's reasonable; he's starving. The answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God." Bread matters, but a person is more than a stomach. Second, a leap. The devil takes him to the highest point of the Temple and says throw yourself down, quoting a psalm about angels catching him. Even scripture can be used as bait. Jesus answers: you shall not tempt the Lord your God. Don't force God to prove himself. Third, everything. From a very high mountain, all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, if he bows down once. The answer: "Begone, Satan: for it is written, The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve." All three answers come from the book of Deuteronomy, from Moses speaking to Israel after forty years in the wilderness. Israel was tested in the desert for forty years; Jesus for forty days, answering with Israel's own words. The Church builds a season on this story. Lent is forty days, and on its first Sunday the Gospel is the temptation in the desert. Catholics fast and give things up then, not because comfort is bad, but to find out what they're really living on.
screen: `STONES INTO BREAD.` · `THROW YOURSELF DOWN.` · `ALL THE KINGDOMS, FOR ONE BOW.` · `THREE ANSWERS FROM DEUTERONOMY.` · then, large: `NOT IN BREAD ALONE DOTH MAN LIVE.`

segments.voice: Run through the three offers once more: bread, the easy comfort; the leap, the need for proof; the kingdoms, getting your way. Notice which one tugs hardest today, if any does, and name it without judging, the way you'd name the weather. Then ask gently what else you're hungry for, and if you pray, bring that hunger to God.
Temptation. Three offers from the tempter in the desert, each met with words from scripture.
Your line: not by bread alone. Forty days, three offers, three answers. Rest now; the lake comes next.

screen: `DAY 33 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LAUNCH OUT INTO THE DEEP.`

34.title: Launch out into the deep (Luke 5:1–11)
34.hook: Peter has fished all night for nothing and lets down the nets once more
34.howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass in the Lectionary's year of Luke, and "duc in altum" is a much-quoted motto since John Paul II used it in his 2001 letter for the new millennium.

segments.voice: Yesterday: temptation, three offers in the desert and three answers from scripture. Not by bread alone.

Morning on the lake of Genesareth, the Sea of Galilee. Two boats pulled up on the shore, the fishermen out of them, washing their nets. Simon and his partners have worked from dark to dawn and caught nothing. Not a small catch: nothing. They're tired, and they want to go home. Then a crowd arrives, pressing around a teacher, and the teacher steps into Simon's boat.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `WASHING THE EMPTY NETS.` → `A TEACHER STEPS INTO THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: Jesus asks Simon to push out a little from the land, and teaches the crowd from the boat. Then he turns to Simon and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught." Simon is the expert here. He knows the lake, and he's just spent the whole night on it. His answer is honest, and a little tired: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net." That but is the hinge. Not because I think it'll work. Because you said so. The nets fill so full they start to break. They wave to their partners in the other boat, James and John, and both boats fill until they begin to sink. Simon doesn't celebrate. He falls at Jesus's knees: depart from me, for I am a sinful man. The catch has frightened him, not with danger, but with nearness. Jesus answers: fear not, from now on you'll be catching people. They bring the boats to land, leave everything, and follow him. In the Latin Bible the line opens with three short words, duc in altum, and Pope John Paul the Second used them to open the new millennium, calling the whole Church to launch out into the deep. Simon, of course, is the one the Church will call Peter.
screen: `LAUNCH OUT INTO THE DEEP.` · `NOTHING ALL NIGHT. BUT AT THY WORD.` · `NETS BREAKING, BOATS SINKING.` · `DEPART FROM ME. FEAR NOT.` · then, large: `DUC IN ALTUM.`

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that you've stopped trying at: a conversation that never goes well, a habit you keep failing to start, a hope you put down. Hold it next to Simon's sentence: I've worked all night and caught nothing, but I'll let down the net. If you pray, offer the trying to God.
Draught. An old word for a catch of fish: what filled Simon's nets when he tried once more at Jesus's word.
Your line: but at thy word. Not sure it'll work, and letting down the net anyway. Six days into week five.

35.title: The wine ran out (John 2:1–11)
35.hook: at a wedding in Cana Mary tells the servants whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye
35.howItsDone: Catholics pray the wedding at Cana as the second Luminous Mystery of the rosary and often read it at weddings; Mary's words to the servants are a favorite line for describing her role of pointing to her son.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tired fisherman said but at thy word, and the nets nearly broke with a great draught. Day thirty-five, the last day of the week, ends at a party.

A village wedding in Galilee. Not an afternoon reception: a feast, guests eating and drinking, the family's honor riding on every cup. Jesus is there, with his first few followers. His mother is there too. Then, somewhere in the middle of it, the thing a host dreads: the wine runs out. The guests don't know yet. The bridegroom may not know yet. But someone has noticed. Not the host, not the steward. Mary.
screen: `A VILLAGE WEDDING FEAST.` → `THE WINE RUNS OUT.` → `MARY NOTICES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Mary goes to her son with four words, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." She doesn't tell him what to do. She just names the need. His answer sounds cool to our ears: "Woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come." Woman wasn't rude in his language; it's the same word he'll use for her from the cross. But he's saying: this isn't my moment. Mary doesn't argue. She turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Then she steps out of the story. Six stone water jars stand there, for the Jewish washing rites, holding two or three measures apiece, John says. A great deal of water. Jesus tells the servants to fill them, and they fill them to the brim. Draw some out, he says, and take it to the chief steward. The steward tastes it, doesn't know where it came from, and calls the bridegroom over, puzzled: everyone serves the good wine first, and the cheap stuff once people have had plenty. "But thou hast kept the good wine until now." Six jars of it. John calls this the beginning of his signs. Catholics treasure it for Mary's sake. Her words to the servants are the last John's Gospel gives her, and they point away from herself. Here Catholics see why they ask Mary to pray for them: she notices the need, brings it to her son, and tells everyone else to listen to him. It's the second Luminous Mystery of the rosary.
screen: `THEY HAVE NO WINE.` · `MY HOUR IS NOT YET COME.` · `SIX JARS, FILLED TO THE BRIM.` · `THE GOOD WINE, KEPT UNTIL NOW.` · then, large: `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU, DO YE.`

segments.voice: This week ran from a boy lost for three days, through the hidden years, the voice in the desert, the baptism, forty days hungry and the nets at dawn, to the wine. Think of the rooms you'll be in today, home, work, a group chat, and look for a need nobody has named: someone running out of patience, money, company or hope. If you pray, you can do what Mary did and simply say it: they have no wine.
Cana. The village in Galilee where Jesus turned water to wine at a wedding, his mother noticing first.
Your line: do whatever he tells you. Next week: healings and encounters. Week five, done.

fork.setup: you're Mary. the wine has run out. you've told your son, and he's said his hour hasn't come. what do you do next?
options: drop it. he said no.
tell the servants to do whatever he tells them.
go and find more wine yourself.
fork.reveal: she turns to the servants: “Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.” and the water jars are filled.

original.note: Greek: woman, a respectful form of address. Jesus calls his mother this at Cana and again from the cross.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus turns water into wine at a party.
what it means: a mother notices a need no one has named, brings it to her son, and tells everyone to listen to him.
what a scholar hears: John calls it the first of the signs; six stone jars, two or three measures apiece, filled to the brim.
